summary: This standards-track memo defines a location object format, extending the Presence Information Data Format (PIDF), for carrying geographical information. It inherits privacy-sensitive properties of PIDF.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a standard way to write down where something is so it can be sent over the internet with privacy rules attached.

questions: what is the geopriv location object
how does geopriv protect location privacy
subtitle: An XML format that wraps a location in a presence document together with the sender's privacy rules.

tldr.problem: Applications share where people are, but a location sent without the owner's preferences or strong protection can be disclosed contrary to what the user wants.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC extends the XML Presence Information Data Format (PIDF) with a geopriv element that holds location information plus usage rules, and requires S/MIME to protect the whole document.
tldr.outcome: A location object that can carry GML or civic locations together with retransmission and retention limits. It is a Proposed Standard that was later updated by RFC 5139, RFC 5491 and RFC 7459.

today: RFC 4119 is a Proposed Standard, published in December 2005, and it has been updated by RFC 5139, RFC 5491 and RFC 7459. Check those updates for changes to the format.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Location information describes a physical position that may be the past, present or future location of a person, event or device. Sharing it is useful for mapping and friend-finding, but the RFC warns that applications may disclose someone's whereabouts against their preferences. Causes include poor protocol security that lets eavesdroppers capture location, and no way to express user preferences.

Because presence information has similar needs for selective distribution and security, this RFC extends the XML-based Presence Information Data Format (PIDF) to carry location. It does not invent a new way to describe a position. It defines an object that encapsulates existing location formats and adds security and policy controls.

The object can be used independently of any using protocol, and any protocol that can carry XML or MIME types can carry PIDF. Full rulesets are out of scope, and the RFC assumes other protocols such as HTTP will move them between Rule Holders and Location Servers.
sections.plainLanguage: It is an envelope for saying where someone is. The envelope also carries a note about who may see it and for how long.

sections.title: Baseline PIDF Usage
sections.content:
The entity attribute of the PIDF presence element holds the URI of whoever the location describes (the presentity). It generally uses the pres URI scheme, and such URIs can serve as unlinkable pseudonyms.

Other PIDF parts keep their usual role. The contact element is optional, so location can be given with no means of communication. The optional timestamp records when the document was created. The mandatory status element may include basic (OPEN or CLOSED), though that is not needed here. A tuple element carries an id so changes can be tracked over time, and holds timestamp, status and contact.
sections.plainLanguage: The name on the envelope says who the location is about. It can be a made-up name, so people cannot easily link it back to them.

sections.title: The geopriv Element and Its Parts
sections.content:
The extension adds a complex geopriv element to PIDF's status. It has two mandatory subelements, location-info and usage-rules, so the rules are clearly tied to the location. Any other subelements are allowed for extensibility, and two optional ones are defined: method and provided-by.

location-info holds one or more chunks of location, and the PIDF document MUST import the XML Schema for each format used. The mandatory baseline is Geography Markup Language (GML) 3.0, and only support for its feature.xsd schema is REQUIRED. Implementations MAY also support the civicLoc format defined in the RFC, with elements such as country, A1 to A6, HNO, FLR and PC. Both formats may appear in the same location-info.

method says how the location was derived, for example gps. provided-by names the entity that supplied it, using an IANA-registered XML namespace. The RFC says most entities should not use it, since the certificate's subjectAltName already identifies the supplier and the element can leak extra information, such as narrowing a state-level location to a small area.
sections.plainLanguage: Inside the envelope there is a place for the location and a place for the rules, and both must be there. Optionally you can also write how you found the location and who told you.

sections.title: Usage Rules
sections.content:
Every geopriv element MUST contain one usage-rules element, even when all fields keep their defaults. Its fields are all optional.

  • retransmission-allowed: when no, the recipient may not share the location or the object with others. The default MUST be assumed to be no, and implementations MUST include the field with no if the Rule Maker states no preference.
  • retention-expires: an absolute date after which the recipient may no longer keep the location. The default is twenty-four hours from the timestamp, or from receipt if there is none. A recipient that receives an already expired object MUST discard it immediately.
  • ruleset-reference: a URI to a fuller ruleset. It SHOULD use HTTPS, and the server MUST authenticate any access. It MAY use a CID URI that points to a MIME body, which SHOULD be encrypted and signed.
  • note-well: human-readable privacy directives not meant for automatic processing.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules say: do not pass this on, throw it away by a certain time, and here is where to read the long version. The default is the safest choice: do not pass it on.

sections.title: Securing the Location Object
sections.content:
The RFC secures the PIDF document as a whole, not element by element, because partial protection could leak privacy. It uses MIME-level security: implementations that support the location extensions MUST support S/MIME and the CMS EnvelopedData and SignedData content types, and MUST implement AES for S/MIME. They SHOULD support X.509 certificates and MUST support password-based CMS encryption. When certificates sign location objects, the subjectAltName SHOULD use the pres URI scheme.

One deployment idea is for Location Servers to hold certificates and share secrets with Generators and Recipients, so a server can use password-based encryption toward a recipient without a certificate. Because Location Servers may need to coarsen a location on the Rule Maker's behalf, a Generator MAY encrypt so the server can decrypt it, and the server can then re-sign the modified object.

The Security Considerations section points to the threat analysis and requirements in RFC 3693 and leaves using-protocol security, such as authenticating subscribers, out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The whole envelope is sealed and signed, not just parts of it. A helper at the post office is allowed to open it only to make the address less exact, then seal it again.

sections.title: Example Location Objects
sections.content:
The RFC gives two PIDF documents for the target pres:geotarget@example.com. The first has a GML Point for San Francisco with retransmission-allowed set to no and a retention-expiry time. The second uses civicAddress with country US, A1 New York, A6 Broadway, HNO 123, LOC Suite 75 and postal code 10027-0401, with retransmission set to yes.

PIDF may be carried as a MIME body with the content type application/pidf+xml, for example in SMTP, HTTP or SIP.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples are filled-in envelopes: one gives a dot on a map with a strict do-not-share rule, and the other gives a street address.

sections.title: IANA Registries and Namespaces
sections.content:
The RFC asks IANA to create a registry of method tokens, open to any party on a first-come-first-serve basis. It pre-registers 7 tokens: GPS, A-GPS, Manual, DHCP, Triangulation, Cell and 802.11.

It also asks for a registry of XML namespaces for provided-by, where new entries MUST be reviewed by an Expert Reviewer designated by the IESG. One namespace is pre-registered: the dataProvider namespace in the appendix, developed by the US National Emergency Number Administration (NENA) for next-generation emergency communications. Finally, it registers the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:pidf:geopriv10.
sections.plainLanguage: There is an official list of allowed ways to say how the location was found, such as GPS or a Wi-Fi access point, so everyone uses the same words.

viz.caption: WHERE GEOPRIV SITS INSIDE A PIDF DOCUMENT

items.title: location-info
items.text: Mandatory. One or more chunks of location, GML baseline or civicLoc.

items.title: usage-rules
items.text: Mandatory. Retransmission, retention, ruleset reference and a note.

items.title: method
items.text: Optional. How the location was derived, from an IANA registry.

items.title: provided-by
items.text: Optional. Who supplied it, from a registered XML namespace.
